topics.title: Compound measures: speed, density and pressure
topics.intro: Speed, density and pressure each combine two measurements: distance per hour, mass per cm³, force per m². Learn one formula and you can rearrange it for the other two quantities.
topics.teach: Explain how to change 72 km/h into metres per second.
topics.talk: On a car journey, ask {her} to work out the average speed from the distance and the time taken.

topics.title: Converting units, including area and volume
topics.intro: Length units scale by 10, 100 or 1000. Area units scale by the square of that, and volume units by the cube: 1 m² is 10,000 cm², and 1 m³ is a million cm³.
topics.teach: Explain why 1 m² is not 100 cm².
topics.talk: Ask {her} how many litres a 1 m by 1 m by 1 m box would hold.

topics.title: Significant figures, error intervals and bounds
topics.intro: A measurement rounded to the nearest unit could be up to half a unit either side. Bounds tell you the range a true value could lie in, and how big or small an answer could really be.
topics.teach: Explain why the upper bound of 34 cm (to the nearest cm) is 34.5 cm even though 34.5 itself would round up.
topics.talk: Ask {her} the shortest a 1.6 m tall person could really be, if the height is given to 1 decimal place.

topics.title: Estimation
topics.intro: Round every number to 1 significant figure and you can estimate almost any calculation in your head. It is the best check that a calculator answer is sensible.
topics.teach: Explain why dividing by 0.2 gives a bigger answer than you started with.
topics.talk: At the shops, ask {her} to estimate the total before the till does.

topics.title: Number bases: binary, base 5 and hexadecimal
topics.intro: We count in tens because we have ten fingers. Computers count in twos, the Babylonians in sixties. In any base, each column is worth the base times the column to its right.
topics.teach: Explain how to convert 45 into binary.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what 10 means in binary, and why.

topics.title: Laws of indices with algebra
topics.intro: The index laws work for letters as well as numbers: multiply and the indices add, divide and they subtract, and a power of a power multiplies. They also let you solve equations like 2ˣ = 32.
topics.teach: Explain why (3x²)³ is 27x⁶ and not 3x⁶.
topics.talk: Ask {her} to solve 2ˣ = 1024 without a calculator.

topics.title: Algebraic fractions
topics.intro: Algebraic fractions follow exactly the same rules as number fractions: cancel common factors, and use a common denominator to add. The trick is to factorise first, then cancel.
topics.teach: Explain why you cannot cancel the x in {{x + 3/x}}.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what {{x/2}} + {{x/3}} is, and how {she} knows.

topics.title: Harder factorising and expanding
topics.intro: Factorise fully by taking out the highest common factor, letters included. Watch for the difference of two squares: a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b).
topics.teach: Explain how to factorise x² − 81 and why it works.
topics.talk: Ask {her} to work out 99 × 101 in {her} head using the difference of two squares.

topics.title: Equations with fractions, and forming equations
topics.intro: Clear fractions by multiplying every term by the denominator (or the LCM). In word problems, the hard part is turning the story into an equation: name the unknown, then write down what you know.
topics.teach: Explain how to solve {{x + 2/3}} = {{x − 1/2}}.
topics.talk: Make up an age puzzle for {her}: “I am three times your age plus 2…”

topics.title: Trial and improvement, and iteration
topics.intro: Some equations can’t be rearranged. Instead, home in on the answer: try values, or feed each answer back into a formula until the numbers settle down.
topics.teach: Explain how you know a solution of x³ + x = 20 lies between 2 and 3.
topics.talk: On a calculator, start with 1 and keep working out 1 + 1 ÷ (the last answer). Ask {her} what number it settles on (the golden ratio!).

topics.title: Functions and inverse functions
topics.intro: A function is a machine: put x in, get f(x) out. The inverse function undoes it, and a composite function feeds one machine into another.
topics.teach: Explain how to find the inverse of f(x) = 3x − 5.
topics.talk: Play “guess my function”: {she} gives inputs, you give outputs.

topics.title: Graphs of quadratics, cubics and reciprocals
topics.intro: Not every graph is a straight line. Quadratics make U-shaped parabolas, cubics make S-shapes and reciprocals make two separate curves that never touch the axes.
topics.teach: Explain how to find the turning point of y = (x − 3)² + 1.
topics.talk: Throw a ball and ask {her} what shape its path makes.

topics.title: Distance–time and real-life graphs
topics.intro: On a distance–time graph the gradient is the speed, a flat section means stopped, and a line sloping down means heading back.
topics.teach: Explain how to find an average speed for a journey that includes a stop.
topics.talk: Sketch a distance–time graph of the school run together.

topics.title: Similarity: lengths, areas and volumes
topics.intro: Similar shapes are enlargements of each other. If lengths are multiplied by k, areas are multiplied by k² and volumes by k³: double a statue’s height and it needs eight times the bronze.
topics.teach: Explain why doubling the lengths of a cube multiplies its volume by 8.
topics.talk: Ask {her} how much more paint a model twice the size would need.

topics.title: Circles: arcs and sectors
topics.intro: A sector is a fraction of a circle: {{θ/360}} of it. So its arc is {{θ/360}} of the circumference and its area is {{θ/360}} of the circle’s area.
topics.teach: Explain how to find the perimeter of a sector.
topics.talk: Cut a pizza into 8 equal slices and ask {her} for the angle of each slice.

topics.title: Angles in polygons with algebra
topics.intro: Combine angle facts with algebra: write the angle sum as an equation, solve for x, then check that every angle makes sense.
topics.teach: Explain how to find the number of sides of a regular polygon from one interior angle.
topics.talk: Ask {her} why a regular polygon can’t have an interior angle of 100°.

topics.title: Column vectors
topics.intro: A column vector says how far to move across (top) and up (bottom). Vectors add top-with-top and bottom-with-bottom, and multiplying by a number stretches them.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between the vectors AB and BA.
topics.talk: Give {her} a treasure-map route as vectors and ask where it ends up.

topics.title: Sets and Venn diagrams
topics.intro: A set is a collection of things. ∩ means “and” (in both), ∪ means “or” (in either), and A′ means “not in A”. Venn diagrams show it all at once.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between A ∩ B and A ∪ B.
topics.talk: Sort the family into “likes tea” and “likes coffee” on a Venn diagram.

topics.title: Systematic counting and the product rule
topics.intro: If one choice can be made in m ways and the next in n ways, there are m × n ways altogether. Count carefully when order matters, and divide when it doesn’t.
topics.teach: Explain why 5 people can stand in a line in 120 different orders.
topics.talk: Ask {her} how many different 4-digit PINs there are, and how long it would take to try them all.

topics.title: Tree diagrams
topics.intro: Tree diagrams show two events one after another. Multiply along the branches for “and”; add the routes for “or”. Without replacement, the second set of branches changes.
topics.teach: Explain how taking a counter without replacing it changes the second probabilities.
topics.talk: Ask {her} for the probability of drawing two aces from a pack of cards, one after the other.

topics.title: Quartiles, interquartile range and box plots
topics.intro: The median splits data in half; the quartiles split it into quarters. The interquartile range measures how spread out the middle half is, and box plots show it at a glance.
topics.teach: Explain why the IQR is often better than the range for comparing data.
topics.talk: Ask {her} to compare two sets of test results: which was better on average, and which was more consistent?

topics.title: Direct and inverse proportion
topics.intro: Direct proportion: y = kx (double one, double the other). Inverse proportion: y = {{k/x}} (double one, halve the other). Find k first, then use it.
topics.teach: Explain how to tell from a table whether two quantities are in inverse proportion.
topics.talk: Ask {her}: if 4 people paint a fence in 6 hours, how long would 3 people take?

topics.title: Constructions, loci and congruence
topics.intro: With just a straight edge and compasses you can bisect lines and angles and construct triangles, exactly as Euclid described. A locus is the set of all points that obey a rule.
topics.teach: Explain how to construct the perpendicular bisector of a line.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what shape the locus of points 1 m from a dog’s stake is.

topics.title: Completing the square and the quadratic formula
topics.intro: When a quadratic won’t factorise, complete the square or use the formula x = {{−b ± √(b² − 4ac)/2a}}. The part under the square root, the discriminant, tells you how many solutions there are.
topics.teach: Explain how completing the square proves the quadratic formula.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what happens to the formula when b² − 4ac is negative.

topics.title: Surds
topics.intro: A surd is a root that can’t be simplified to a whole number, like √2. Simplify by taking out square factors: √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2.
topics.teach: Explain how to rationalise the denominator of {{6/√3}}.
topics.talk: Ask {her} why √2 × √2 is exactly 2, even though √2 never ends as a decimal.

topics.title: Geometric sequences
topics.intro: In a geometric sequence you multiply by the same number each time: the common ratio. Its nth term is a × rⁿ⁻¹, and it grows (or shrinks) very fast.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between an arithmetic and a geometric sequence.
topics.talk: The legend of the chessboard: 1 grain of rice on the first square, 2 on the next, then 4, 8… Ask {her} how many grains go on the 64th square.

topics.title: 3D Pythagoras and the cosine rule
topics.intro: Pythagoras works in three dimensions too: the space diagonal of a cuboid satisfies d² = a² + b² + c². For triangles without a right angle, the cosine rule extends Pythagoras.
topics.teach: Explain how to find the longest rod that fits in a box.
topics.talk: Measure a shoebox and ask {her} to predict the length of its space diagonal before measuring it.

topics.title: Algebraic proof
topics.intro: A proof shows something is true for every number, not just the ones you tried. Use 2n for an even number, 2n + 1 for an odd one and n, n + 1 for consecutive integers.
topics.teach: Prove that the difference between the squares of two consecutive integers is always odd.
topics.talk: Ask {her} to prove that the sum of any two odd numbers is even.

items.prompt: Daedalus wants every point that is the same distance from two pillars, A and B. What does he construct?

options.text: A circle centred on the midpoint of AB
options.feedback: A circle gives points the same distance from ONE point.
Points on AB are mostly closer to one pillar than the other.

options.text: The bisector of the angle at A
options.feedback: Angle bisectors are about being equidistant from two LINES.

items.explain: Points equidistant from two points lie on the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them.

items.prompt: Which construction gives every point that is the same distance from two walls meeting at a corner?

options.text: The angle bisector of the corner
The perpendicular bisector of the walls
options.feedback: That is for two POINTS, not two lines.
A circle gives points the same distance from the corner itself.

options.text: A line parallel to one wall
options.feedback: That keeps a fixed distance from only one wall.

items.explain: Points equidistant from two intersecting lines lie on the bisector of the angle between them.

items.prompt: A goat is tied to a stake with a 5 m rope. What shape is the boundary of the region it can reach?

options.feedback: Every direction is equally far: that makes a circle.
It can move in every direction.
Only if something blocks half of the field.

items.explain: The locus of points a fixed distance from a point is a circle.

items.prompt: What is the locus of points exactly 2 cm from a straight line segment AB?

options.text: Two parallel lines joined by semicircles (a “stadium”)
Two parallel lines, 2 cm either side of AB
options.feedback: Near the ends A and B the points curve round.
A circle is for a single point.

options.text: An ellipse with A and B as its two foci
options.feedback: The long sides are straight lines, not the curve of an ellipse.

items.explain: Alongside the segment the points lie on two parallel lines; round each end they form semicircles centred on A and B.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT enough to prove two triangles congruent?

options.feedback: SSS does prove congruence.

options.text: SAS: two sides and the angle between them
options.feedback: SAS does prove congruence.

options.text: RHS: right angle, hypotenuse and one side
options.feedback: RHS does prove congruence.

items.explain: Three equal angles only prove the triangles are SIMILAR: one could be an enlargement of the other.

items.prompt: Why is SSA (two sides and an angle that is NOT between them) not a congruence condition?

options.text: The same data can fit two different triangles
It only works for right-angled triangles
options.feedback: SSA fails for many kinds of triangle, not just right-angled ones.

options.text: It needs all three angles to be known as well
options.feedback: Three angles fix the shape but not the size, so they don’t help here.

options.text: It is the same as SAS
options.feedback: The position of the angle matters: SAS has it BETWEEN the sides.

items.explain: With the angle not between the two sides, the third side can often swing into two positions: the “ambiguous case”.

items.prompt: A cylinder stands upright on a table. What is its plan view (from directly above)?

options.feedback: That is its front elevation.
A cone’s side view is a triangle.
A cube’s plan is a square.

items.explain: Plan = from above; front elevation = from the front; side elevation = from the side. An upright cylinder: the plan is a circle, the elevations are rectangles.

items.prompt: A square-based pyramid like those at Giza is viewed from the front. What shape is its front elevation?

options.feedback: That is its plan (from above, with its diagonals).
Nothing about a pyramid is round.
A square-based pyramid has five faces, but the front view is a triangle.

items.explain: From the front you see a triangle; from above, a square with its diagonals.

items.prompt: Euclid’s constructions allowed only two tools. Which two?

options.text: A straight edge and a pair of compasses
A ruler with measurements and a protractor
options.feedback: Euclid used no measurements: just a straight edge and compasses.

options.text: A set square and a calculator
options.feedback: Calculators came over two thousand years later.
No protractor: angles were bisected with compasses.

items.explain: Greek geometers constructed everything with an unmarked straight edge and compasses.

items.prompt: Two triangles have angles 40°, 60°, 80° and 80°, 40°, 60°. What can you say?

options.text: They are similar (but might not be congruent)

options.feedback: Equal angles don’t fix the size.
They have the same three angles, so they are similar.

options.text: One must be a reflection of the other
options.feedback: Equal angles show similarity, nothing more.

items.explain: Equal angles mean the same shape: similar. Congruent also needs a matching side.

items.prompt: Which proves that the difference between the squares of two consecutive integers is always odd?

options.feedback: Examples, however many, are not a proof.
Expand carefully: (n + 1)² = n² + 2n + 1.
Expand carefully: it is −2n − 1, and the order was reversed.

items.explain: (n + 1)² − n² = n² + 2n + 1 − n² = 2n + 1. Any integer of the form 2n + 1 is odd.

items.prompt: How do you prove that the sum of two odd numbers is always even?

options.feedback: Examples don’t prove “always”.
That only covers adding an odd number to itself: use different letters.
That is false: 3 + 5 = 8.

items.explain: Use different letters for two different odd numbers: 2a + 1 and 2b + 1. Their sum is 2(a + b + 1).

items.prompt: Theo claims: “The product of two consecutive even numbers is always a multiple of 8.” Which is the key step in a proof?

options.feedback: Examples support a claim but don’t prove it.
Those are the same number, not consecutive even numbers.
8 IS a multiple of 8.

items.explain: 2n(2n + 2) = 4n(n + 1). One of n and n + 1 is even, so n(n + 1) = 2k and the product is 8k.

items.prompt: Kit says: “n² + n + 41 is prime for every whole number n.” How can you disprove it?

options.text: Find one n where it fails: n = 40 gives 41²
Show it works for n = 1, 2 and 3, then generalise
options.feedback: Examples that work can never disprove a claim.

options.text: Use algebra to show it is always odd
options.feedback: Odd numbers aren’t necessarily prime.
One counterexample is enough.

items.explain: A single counterexample disproves an “always” claim. n = 40: 1600 + 40 + 41 = 1681 = 41².

items.prompt: Which shows that (n + 3)² − (n − 3)² is always a multiple of 12?

options.feedback: Expand both brackets: n² + 6n + 9 − (n² − 6n + 9).
The n² and the 9 cancel when you subtract.

items.explain: (n² + 6n + 9) − (n² − 6n + 9) = 12n, and 12n is a multiple of 12 for any integer n.

options.text: checking every possible case, when there are only a few
trying lots of examples until you get tired
options.feedback: It must cover EVERY case, not just many.
That is a general (algebraic) proof.
That disproves, rather than proves.

items.explain: For example: every square number ends in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. Check the last digit of each of 0², 1², …, 9² and you have covered every case.

items.prompt: Mira says the sum of three consecutive integers is always a multiple of 3. Which is a correct algebraic proof?

options.feedback: Those aren’t consecutive.
An example, not a proof.
Check the arithmetic: it is 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1).

items.explain: Choosing the middle number as n makes it neat: (n − 1) + n + (n + 1) = 3n.

items.prompt: The Pythagoreans discovered that √2 is irrational. The classic proof that it can’t be a fraction works by…

options.text: exhaustion: checking every possible fraction a/b
options.feedback: There are infinitely many fractions to check.

options.text: a counterexample: one fraction that fails
options.feedback: Counterexamples disprove claims.
No measurement can prove irrationality.

items.explain: If √2 = {{a/b}} then a² = 2b², so a is even; then b is even too, contradicting “lowest terms”. So no such fraction exists.
